PREFACE. 



The fourth volume of the Testamenta Eboracensia 
covers a period of about twenty-five years, and brings 
the series down to the commencement of the reign 
of Henry VIII. It has been found impossible to 
travel more quickly over a field which is so crowded 
with interesting documents. At the same time, the 
Editor has not scrupled to abridge his materials where 
curtailment was practicable, and all formal and 
valueless details have been generally discarded. 

The next volume ought to extend, if possible, over 
the reign of Henry VIII., but the reader will find 
that after the beginning of the sixteenth century the 
Wills preserved at York become gradually less in- 
teresting. At the same time, as evidences for the 
genealogist, they lose not a tittle of their value; nay, 
that value increases as we near the period at which 
the Heralds began to hold their Visitations. But we 
may look in vain for the quaint verbiage of the pre- 
ceding reigns, and for the minute enumeration of the 
testator's wealth and substance which was previously 
so common. 

The question has been asked more than once, Why 
is there not a glossary to each of these volumes of 



357524 



VI PREFACE. 



Wills ? The reason is this. In a work peculiarly 
devoted to genealogy it seemed inadvisable to intro- 
duce among the illustrative notes any explanations 
of dialects or language. The genealogical notes of 
themselves take up all the space that could be spared 
for illustration. And no glossary has been appended 
to these volumes, because it is the intention of the 
Society before long to take this subject in hand on a 
much larger scale. Great preparations have already 
been made for a glossary of northern words in use 
prior to the reign of Queen Anne. To construct this, 
the greater part of the volumes that the Society has 
published will be laid under contribution, and the 
work will be supplemented and illustrated by MS. 
evidences of undoubted authority, and also, in some 
cases, by the printed works of northern writers. 

For the notes to which the initials of R. H. S. are 
appended the Editor is indebted to the kindness and 
local research of Mr. Skaife. That gentleman has 
also added to the value of this volume by a capital 
index, which he has prepared with his customary 
skill. Nor must Messrs. Hudson and Buckle be 
passed over. They are always ready to throw open 
the treasures in their office for the benefit of this 
Society, and the Editor has always been welcomed by 
them with unvarying courtesy and attention. 

J. R. 

York, October, 1869.

* Inasmuch as the volumes of the Testamenta Eboracensia contain almost all 
the wills of the Scropes of Bolton and Masham, it has been thought proper to 
supplement the series with two or three others which have been derived from 
other sources. This will of Richard, third Lord Scrope of Bolton, has only 
been known through some inaccurate and meagre extracts. It was also entered 
in one of the missing Registers of the Archdeacons of Richmond. 

The testator made his will during the siege of Rouen, and died in 1420, aged 
only 27. His wife was a daughter of Ralph, Earl of Westmorland, and by her 
he had two sons. (Scrope and Grosvenor Roll, 69, 60.)

1 1 am able to make a few contributions towards a life of this distinguished 
man. Nothing has hitherto been collected about him :— 

He was a younger son of Sir Ralph Lumley by Eleanor, daughter of John Lord 
Neville of Raby. (Surtees, ii. 162.) Fuller says that he was educated at Trin. Hall, 
Cambridge (Hist. Univ. Cant. 48); at all events he was Master there in 1429 (Le 
Neve, iii. 679), and Chancellor of the Univ. in 1427. (Ibid. iii. 600.') To Queen's 
Coll. he gave 2002. and many books (Lelandi Coll. v. 226), the same sum 
and many books to Jesus Coll. in 1459: and in 1448 he gave 220/. towards the 
building of the college, and a Bible in three volumes. (Hist Univ. Cant. i. 245-7.) 

On May 1, 1416, he was coll 4 to the deanery of Lanchester, co. Durham, 
which he exch d on May 22, 1417, with Mr. William Pelleson, for the rectory of 
Anderby, co. Lincoln. (Reg. Langley at Durham, 95*.) On May 21, 1420, he 
was inst* to the rectory of Warton, in Westmorland, which he res 4 the next 
year. (MS. Harl. 6978, 17a.) On 27 Mar., 1422, he was coll d to the archdeaconry 
of Northumberland. (Reg. Langley, 112 a.) 

On Jan. 26, 1423-4, ne was inst* to the rectory of Hawarden and the prebend of 
Saltmarsh, at Howden, exchr for them with Henry Merston, his rectory of 
Charine. (Reg. Ebor. tede vac. 337 b.) On Dec 12, 1424, he was inst* to the 
mastership of Bootham hospital, York, and a prebend at Osmotherley, in 
exchange for his stall at Saltmarsh, with Robert Frende. (Ibid. 370 a.) In 1425 
he was made precentor at Lincoln. (Le Neve, ii. 84.) This, together with the 
archdeaconry of Northumberland, he exch d on Nov. 8, 1427, with Robert Burton 
for the rectories of Stepney, and Burmarsh in Kent (Reg. Langley, 133 a; New- 
court, i. 739.) On May 9, 1429, he was ins td to the rectory of Baynton, co. York, 
at the pres* of Matilda Lady Mauley. (Reg. Kempe, 7b.) 

On Jan. 27, 1429-30, Martin V. made Lumley bishop of Carlisle ; and on Apr. 
16, 1430, by leave of the archbishop of Canterbury, he was consecrated in tne 
chapel belonging to the hospital of St Thomas at Eastbridge, near Canterbury,

On Dec. 3, previous, it was agreed in Parliament that the royal assent to his ap- 
pointment should be given, the Duke of Gloucester and Lord Scrope objecting. 
(Acts and Ord. of the Pr. Council, iv. 8.) On May 1, 1433, he had letters of pro- 
tection to go to the Council at Basle. (Feed. x. 650.) On July 12, 1434, he was ap- 
pointed to treat with James, king of Scotland (Ibid. 596), and he was afterwards 
engaged in Scottish affairs. (Ibid. 621—629.) From 1447 to 1450 he was Lord 
Treasurer of England. (Dugd. Chron. 64.) In 1449-50 he was translated to Lincoln, 
and, on March 18, Thos. Chicheley, archdeacon of Canterbury, was ordered to 
instal him. (MS. Harl. 6952, 82 a.) He died in the same year and was bur 4 
in the Charterhouse, London. (Coll. Top. iv. 309; Willis, Hi. 57.)

between his said son Adam and Margery his wife, dau. of Sir John de Hotham, 
knt, jun., of Scorbro'. Alice his dau. Margaret his wife is an ox*. [Pr. 18th 
July, 1343.] (Reg. Zouche, 309 b.)

Creyke and widow of John Middleton, of Beverley. Her will occurs afterwards. 
The Hildyards are a very ancient Yorkshire family. A piece of evidence has 
occurred to me in the shape of a suit in the Ecclesiastical Court at York in 1370, 
which places their early history on a new and satisfactory footing. It turns on 
the legality of a marriage between two cousins, which is best represented in a short 
tabular pedigree. One of the witnesses says that the " stirps " of the family 
came from Hildyard in Essex. The accuracy of this account is confirmed by 
that invaluable piece of Yorkshire history, the Liber de Melsa. (See voL ii. 
218-19.)

t The testatrix, who was an aged lady, was a daughter of James Strangeways 
of Skelton esq. (?) Her first husband was Conan Barton, Esq., of Whenby, who

On Dec. 2nd, 1465, Archbishop William Booth allowed her the privilege of an 
oratory at Sedbury, she being then a widow (Reg. William Booth.) On Apr. 30, 
1463, the Archdeacon of Richmond granted permission "honorabili mulieri 
dominie Johanna, relictae Christoferi Boynton armigeri, nuper defuncti," to have 
service in an oratory, wherever she chose. (Reg. Archid. Richmond, 42 b.) On 
March 19, 1473-4, Archbishop Neville granted the same privilege to dame Joan 
Boynton of Yarm for 3 years (Re$. Neville, 163 a.) She seems to have spent 
the latter years of her life at Yarm in works of charity and devotion.

XIV. THE WILL OF SIB RALPH GREYSTOCK KNT., BARON OF 
GREYSTOCK. 

[Reg. Rotherham, 334a.] 

May 27, 1487. Radulphus, dominus de Grastok* et Weme. 
Sep. in cancello monasterii Sancte Trinitatis de Kirkham, coram 
altari. Priori et conventui dicti monasterii, pro sepultura mea, 
die obitus mei, ac pro decimis meis oblitis, cs. Priori dicti 

* A hitherto unknown will of the head of the great baronial house of Grey- 
stock. For an account of the family, see Hodgson's Northumberland, ii. part ii. 
378-9 ; Coll. Top. ii. 160-1. The evidences at York add materially to the informa- 
tion there given. 

The will of his, the testator's, father, who died in 1436, is in Wills and 
Inv. i. 84-6. 

In 1435 the testator married Elizabeth daughter of William Lord Fitzhugh. 
(Test. Ebor. iii. 327-8.) The marriage licence shows the affinity of the two 
contracting parties. He is said to have married, secondly, Elizabeth, daughter of 
John Terell, (Coll. Top. ii. 160,) but his widow's name was Beatrix (Hatcliffe), 
and she re-married Robert Constable, esq., serieant-at-law, in 1490. (Test. 
Ebor. iii. 355.) She survived him, and, taking the vows of chastity in 1501-2, 
(Ibid. 363) made her will in 1505. This is printed afterwards. 

The testator was buried in the noble monastery of Kirkham, of which, by 
inheritance, he was the founder. The chaplets of Greystock still surmount the 
beautiful gateway of the Priory. The ancient manor of Hinderskelf, in which 
the Greystocks lived, has now changed its name to Castle-Howard. 

According to the Coll. Top. the testator had many children. John, one of his 
sons, made a splendid alliance with Cecily daughter of William Herbert, Earl of 
Pembroke. (Test. Ebor. iii. 349.) This was not known before. 

Richard Greystock, another of his sons, took holy orders. On March 10, 
1463-4, he was collated by Archbishop Booth to the rectory of Wheldrake, which 
he resigned in Feb. 1486-7. (Reg. Wm. Booth, 73 ft.) On May 7, 1465, the 
Dean and Chapter of York, sede vacante, granted him letters dimissory. (Reg. 
$ede vacante, 455 ft), and on April 7 in the next year he was allowed to be absent 
from his living two years. (Reg. Geo. Neville, 53 a.) On Dec. 3, 1481, he was 
instituted to the rectory of Brompton, in Pickering Lythe (Reg. Rotherham, 158 a.) 
which he held till his death. (Ibid. 92 ft.) On Feb. 15, 1475-6, he was installed 
prebendary of Welton Brinkhall, at Lincoln. (Le Neve, ii. 229.) On Feb. 24, 
1486-7, he was made succentor canonicorum at York (Reg. Rotherham, 102 ft.), 
and he died holding that office in 1496. 

The following notices are illustrative of the Greystock pedigree. Nov. 25, 
1346, nuncupative will of Elizabet de Graystok. To be buried in the church of 
Butterwick. Sir Ralph de Hastings, knt. sen., and Richard de Neville, rector 
of Scotton, executors. They renounce, and William de Kelk administered. 
(Reg. Zouche, 305 ft.) She was a Neville, and the widow of Robert fitz Ralph, 
lord of Graystock. According to what is called the Greystock Roll, which is 
now before me, " Iste Robertus sepultus est apud Botyrwyk." At Butterwick 
there is an effigy of a knight, which may perhaps commemorate him. Some 
modern churchwardens, anxious to leave a memorial ' of their taste and skill 
even more striking than usual, have set the statue up against the chancel wall, 
whilst, above the head of the figure, they have made an arch of two fragments 
of the rib of a whale. To add to their beauty the bones are duly white-washed I 

On Aug. 3, 1473, administration of Isabella lady Greystock, late wife of Sir 
Ralph Greystock, knt., was granted to Sir Henry Vavasour, knt, Thomas 
Thwaites, and William ScargiU, sen., esqs. (Reg. Test. iv. 199 ft.) Perhaps she 
was a wife of the testator.

XVII. THE WILL OF MR. ROBERT BOTHE, DEAN OF YORK. 
[Reg. Rotherham, 335*.] 

Jan. 23, 1487-8. Robertas Bothe,* decanus eocl. cath. 
Beati (Petri) Ebor. Sep. infra cath. prope sepulerum magistri 
Eicardi Andrew, praedecessoris mei, et cooperiendum cum lapide 

• A son of Sir Robert Booth, of Barton in Lancashire, by Dulcia, or Douce, 
daughter and co-heir of Sir Richard Venables. (Baines* Lancashire, iii. 112.) 
He was one of the widely spreading family of that name which took the church 
of York by storm about this time, and held the great posts within it without any 
regard to decency or propriety. 

On Jan. 10, 1474-6, Mr. Robert Booth, LL.D., was instituted to the living of 
Bowden, diocese of Lincoln, at the presentation of Thomas Lord Scrope. (MS. HarL, 
6952, 104 a.) On Aug. 15 and Oct. 26, 1474, he was one of the commissioners 
appointed to make a treaty with Scotland. (Feed. xi. 824, and Rot Scotiae, ii. 444.) 
On Oct. 27, 1476, he was collated to the prebend of St James, at Beverley. 
(Reg. Laur. Booth, 11a.) On Jan. 14, 1476-7, he was collated to the stall of 
Ampleforth, at York. (Ibid. 7 a.) On Feb. 14, $eq. y he was collated to the pre- 
bend of St. Andrew at Beverley. (Ibid. 11 b.) On Aug. 18, 1477, he was 
elected Dean of York, (Acta. Cap. Ebor.), with which office he held the stall of 
Wetwang, to which he was collated Feb. 14, 1477-8. (Reg. Booth, 4 b.) He was also

One Robert Bothe, of Harlesey, was ordained in 1458, the nnnnery of Erden 
giving him a title, viz., sub-deacon 18th March, deacon 27th May, and priest 23rd 
Sept (Reg. Wm. Booth, ad finem.) Whether he was the Dean or not I cannot

Dean Booth must not be confounded with Thomas Booth who was abbat of 
St. Mary's at the time his namesake held the deanery. (See Curious Discourses, 
i 256.) If other proof were wanting, one circumstance only would disprove the 
identity — a monk could not make a will. 

The Dean's monument was at the south end of the " cross body " of York Minster. 
(Torre, 194.) His epitaph, for a mediaeval one, was exceptionally complimentary:

Thomas Creyke was a son of Alexander Creyke, of Beverley. By will dated 
in 1465, desired to be buried in the church of the Friars Minors, London, 
if he died there ; if he died nearer home, in the church B.M. at Beverley. To 
his daughter Margaret, for her marriage, 40 marks. To his son Thomas, M pro 
inventione sua in curia," 40 marks. To his son Roger, lands in Beverley, worth 
4 marks per annum. " Messuagium meum in Kyllom, quod nuper f nit Will. Dryng, 
in animae meae exonerationem, restituatur rectis haeredibus ejusdem Willelmi." 
Wife Isabel, son Thomas, and George Scalby, executors. [Pr. 4 Sept. 1465.] 
(Reg. Test. iv. 267*.) 

The wife of Alexander Creyke was Isabel, daughter of Thomas White of 
Beverley, clothier.- Her will was proved at York in 1488. (Test. Ebor. ii. 167.) 

Thomas Creyke, the eldest son, seems to have been a lawyer. He left a wife 
and three children, as appears from his inventory, Robert, Anthony, and Agnes.

* The testator was the son and heir of Sir Richard Copley, of Batley, by his 
second wife Elizabeth Harrington. He was a lawyer, and made a large fortune. His 
will is valuable in many respects. He was twice married, according to Mr. 
Hunter : 1. to Margaret, daughter and co-heir of John Saint Loe, of Gunnersby, 
co. Lincoln. (I question this marriage, as it is not mentioned by the testator 
when he mentions the other.) 2. to Margaret, daughter of Sir William 
Ryther of Ryther; but it does not appear that he left children by either. His 
wealth was dispersed among his relatives and friends.

the following summary. It is of great value. " My tenements in Stanley and

Gamaliel Clifton was a distinguished man. At his father's death he must have 
been very young. On Feb. 17, 1499-1500, Mr. Gamaliel Clifton, scholar and 
bachelor of laws, of Clifton, had letters dimissory. (Reg. Rotherham, 267 b.) 
On July 30, 1500, he was instituted to the rectory of Hawton, Notts, on the pre- 
sentation of Thomas Molyneux, esa.. (MS. Cotton, Galba, E. x., 135<i.) On Aug. 
3 in the same year he was admitted to the stall of Wistow at York. (Acta 
Capit Ebor.) On Sept. 19 and Dec. 19, 1500, he was ordained deacon and priest, 
respectively, on the title of his living and stall. (Reg. Arundel at Lichfield, 292.) 
On Feb. 12; 1508-9, he was instituted to the rectory of Wilford, Notts, on the 
presentation of Robert Clifton, of Clifton, esq. (Reg. Savage, 6«.) On 8th 
August, 1522, he was appointed canon of Windsor by patent, a post which he 
held till 1541. (Le Neve, iii. 392.) In 1525 he became prebendary of Pratum 
Minors at Hereford, which he resigned on May 16, 1529, for the prebend of 
Colwell. (Ibid. i. 499-525.) On 5 July, 1529, he was elected dean of Hereford. 
(Ibid. i. 477.) This office, together with the rectory of West Udesley, Berks, and 
other posts and dignities, he held till his death. His will is dated April 28, 
1641, and, dying in that vear, he was buried in Hereford cathedral. (Willis, ii. 
635.) He proceeded bachelor of civil law at Cambridge, and subsequently doctor, 
and supplicated for incorporation at Oxford in 1521. He was of high repute as 
a canonist, and was one of the lawyers who were concerned with the divorces 
between Henry VIII. and Katharine of Arragon and Anne of Cleves. (Ath. 
Cant i. 78, 533. Fiddes's Life of Wolsey, appendix, 203.) 

Silvan Clifton was instituted to the rectory of Clifton on May 30th, 1506 (Reg. 
Savage, 61 a.), and gave it up in 1531 for Norbiton in the diocese of Winchester. 

Hexekiah Clifton lived at Burton Agnes in Yorkshire, and will occur after- 
wards.

A short account of this distinguished, man may be acceptable. At all events 
it will be new. 

He was a member of a Lancashire family, a branch really of the Traffords, 
which afterwards produced two noted men, William Ghaderton, bishop of Chester, 
and Lawrence Chaderton, one of the translators of the Bible. (F.R.R.) He came 
into Yorkshire with archbishop Booth. It is no easy matter to enumerate the 
offices that he held. 

On April, 1460, at a private and special ordination he was ordained acolyte in 
the chapel at Scrooby by John Green, bishop of the Isles, he being of the diocese 
of Coventry and Lichfield. (Beg. Wm. Booth, adjincm.) On 20th Sept teq. he was 
made sub-deacon. (Ibid.) On April 27th, 1462, on the resignation of the prelate 
, just mentioned, he was instituted to the vicarage of Blyth, which he resigned in 
August seq. (Ibid. 96 ft.) On Sept. 20, 1462, he was instituted to the rectory of 
B rough ton, Sir Robert Clifton presenting him. (Ibid. 99 a.) This, on June 20, 
1470, he exchanged for the vicarage of Kirk by Lonsdale. (Beg. archid. Rich- 
mond, 60a.) On Oct 7, 1465, he was made archbishop Neville's receiver for 
Hexhamshire (Reg. Geo. Neville, 40 J), and on Nov. 6, 1466, being that prelate's 
chaplain, he was instituted to the rectory of Hockerton, Notts (Ibid. 35 ft), which 
he resigned in Oct. 1470. On June 26th, 1473, he was instituted to the rectory 
of Staunton, Notts (Ibid. 153a), which he resigned in July, 1478, receiving a 
pension of seven marks per annum out of it. On Jan. 6, 1474-5, he was collated 
to the stall of South Muskham at Southwell, resigning the Sacrist's prebend 
there. (Ibid ii. 3 a.) On Feb. 10, 1475-6, he was collated to the stall of North, 
well, 3rd part, there. (Ibid. 23 ft.) On Nov. 10, 1476, he was collated to a moiety 
of the stall of Oxton cum Crophill in the same church, of which he was a resi- 
dentiary. (Reg. L. Booth, 9a.) On March 29, 1478, he exchanged his prebend 
at St Katharine's altar in Beverley minster for the stall of Stretton, at Salisbury 
(Reg. Laur. Rooth, 11-12), and on Aug. 26, 1478, he was appointed master or 
warden of Sibthorpe college. (Ibid. 46 a.) From 1475 to 1482 he held the stall 
of Welton Ryval at Lincoln. (Le Neve, ii. 234.) 

During the reign of Richard III. Chaderton was in high favour with the king, 
and preferments were showered upon him. On Aug. 14, 1483, he was instituted 
to the rectory of Calverton, Bucks, of the king's gift. (MS. Harl. 433, 143, and 
Lipecombe's Bucks, iv. 86.) The same monarch made him clerk of the hanaper, 
treasurer, and receiver of the chamber, dean of the free chapel at Barking; and 
granted him the wardship and marriage of William, son and heir of George 
Bothe; the farm of the Temple near Marlborough; the lands of William Coling- 
bourae, and the manor of Knesall, Notts. (MS. Harl., ut supra, 32 a, 36 ft, 80 ft, 
950, 99 a, 1030, 104 ft.) In Feb. 1492-3 he was made archdeacon of Chester 
(Le Neve, i. 567), an office which he held during his life. At his death he held 
two other archdeaconries, that of Salisbury, to which he was collated probably 
in 1483 (Le Neve, ii. 625), and that of Totnes at Exeter, to which he was ap 
pointed in 1491. (Le Neve, i. 403.) 

His list of preferments is not yet done. In Aug. 1484 he was collated to the 
prebend of Cadington Minor at London, which he held till he died. (Le Neve, 
ii. 372; Newcourt, i. 131.) On Sept. 25, 1484-6, he was instituted, at the king's 
presentation, to the rectory of Almondbury. (Ibid. 1170.) On Jan. 2, 1484-5, 
he was collated to the prebend of Thorp at Ripon. (Reg. Rotherham, 97 ft.) 
On April 8, 1485, he was collated to the stall of Dunham at Southwell, resigning 
that of Oxton. (Ibid. 98 ft.) In June, 1485, he was made prebendary of Nassing- 
ton at Lincoln. (Le Neve, ii. 193.) On Jan. 30, 1487-8, he was collated to the 
stall of St. Andrew at Beverley. (Reg. Rotherham, 1030.) On July 7th, 1491, 
he was made a collector of the subsidy for the expedition to France. (Feed. xii. 
446.) From 1492 to 1493 he was vicar of Allhallows Barking (Newcourt, i.

f There is little, if anything, known of the testator in the North. This will

I shewed this will to my late kind and lamented friend, to whom Cambridge 
owes so much, Mr. C. H. Cooper, and he sent me the following illustrative notices 
of the testator: — Jan. 30, 1473-4, Robert Belamy, bachelor in decrees, was insti- 
ttued to the church of Malton, co. Cambridge, on the presentation of Sir Thomas 
Tyrell, knt (MS. Baker, xxx. 50.) King's Hall, of which he was a fellow, had 
been founded by Edward III., and was by Henry VIII. absorbed into his great 
foundation of Trinity College. The fellowships, 32 in number, were in the gift 
of the Crown. No one appreciated more than Mr. Cooper the invaluable infor- 
mation that may be derived from wills. 

In the margin of the register in which the will occurs are the words Nota pro 
jurUdictwne domini contra dictum hospitale 8. Leonardi. This refers to the 
question of privilege. 

This will is also registered at Doctors' Commons.

XXXVII. THE WELL OF MR. WILLIAM P0TEMAN, ABCHDEACON OF 
THE EAST RIDING. 

[Reg. Rotheram, 352 «.] 

Febr. 8, 1492-3. Willelmus Poteman,* archidiaconus Est- 
ridding in eccl. metropolitica Ebor. et canonicus residentiarius 
ejusdem. Sep. in eccl. Ebor. prope capollam nbi recolendae 

• The testator was a doctor of laws, a scholar, and an ecclesiastic of wealth 
and high position. 

On Not. 9, 1459, he became warden of All Souls, Oxford, haying been a little 
before the principal of the halls of St George and Woodcock, and moderator of 
the school of Cesarean law. In the same year he was presented by his college 
to the rectory of Stanlake, and from 1459-60 to 1464 he was rector of Elmcley 
(Hist. Univ. Oxon. ir. 26S. Newcourt, i. 210.) On August 21, 1460, he was 
collated to the rectory of Roding Alta in Essex (Newcoart ii. 501), which he 
held for a short time. On Feb. 9, 1465-6, he became prebendary of Empingham 
at Lincoln, and continued so for nine years. (Le Neve, ii. 147.) In 1466 his 
college presented him to the rectory of Treng. (Hist. Univ. Oxon. iv. 268.) 

Whilst Poteman was warden of All Souls, George Neville, bishop of Exeter, 
was chancellor of the University. When that prelate was translated to York 
in 1466, Poteman found in him a munificent patron, and followed him into the 
North. In that year Poteman resigned several of his southern benefices, viz., 
the wardenship of All Souls, the rectory of Chelmsford, and the stall of Sneat- 
ing at London. (Newcoart, i. 210.) At York he was a canon in residence, and 
held the following posts in the church of York ; the stall of Weighton to which 
he was collated Feb. 22, 1466-7. (Reg. Geo. Neville, ha.) This he gave up when 
admitted on Sept. 25, 1470, to that of Barn by. (Acta Capit. sub anno.) On 
Sep. 25, 1470, he was made archdeacon of Cleveland (Ibid.), and was so until 
1484. On Jan. 29, 1474-5, he was collated to the stall of Strensall, which he 
held till he died. (Reg. Geo. Neville, ii. 4 a.)

He held other preferment in the diocese. On March 80, 1467, archbishop 
Neville made Poteman provost of Beverley, in which office he died. (Ibid 5b.) 
He also instituted him on Jan. 2, 1465-6, to the rectory of Settrington, which, 
with the stall of Barn by, be gave np in 1470, in exchange for the archdeaconry 
of Cleveland. (Ibid. 27 b.) The archbishop admitted him to a prebend at Hem- 
ingborongh on Dec. 27, 1466. (Ibid 87 b.) On Nov. 15, 1468, he became vicar- 
general to John Sherwood, archdeacon of Richmond. (Beg. archid. Richmond, 
66 a. b.) In addition to these preferments he was in many ways connected with 
the see of York. In 1466 he was official of the court (Reg. Neville.) On 
June 8, 1475, the archbishop made him supervisor of all his houses, manors, and 
warrens in Yorkshire (Ibid. ii. 18a); and, on three several occasions, viz., on 
April 3rd, 1467, March 2nd, 1474-5, and June 8, $eq. f he appointed him his vicar- 
general. (Ibid. 90a. et $eq.) Indeed it is impossible to examine the register of 
archbishop Neville without seeing that the management of the diocese of York 
was chieflv entrusted to Poteman's care. 

After the death of archbishop Neville, Poteman was not forgotten by his suc- 
cessors in the see. On Feb. 14, 1477-8, he was made prebendary of Nunwick at Ripon 
(Reg. Laur. Booth, 13 a), and master of the hospital of B.M. Magdalen in the same 
town in July, 1479. (Ibid. 52 b.) Thrice, viz. on 30th Aug. 1478, 18th Sept. 1480, 
and in Aug. 1485, he was made official of the court of York (Beg. Booth and 
Botherham), and once, on Sept. 18, 1480, he was made vicar-general to arch- 
bishop Botherham. (Beg. Botnerham, la, b.) On Jan. 13, 1484-5, he was made 
archdeacon of the East Biding (Ibid. 98 a), an office which he filled during his 
life. On March 16, 1471-2, Poteman was appointed to treat with the commis- 
sioners of Scotland about a truce. (Feed. xi. 748, Rot Scot. ii. 434.) On May 16, 
1473, he had the charge of punishing those who broke the truce. (Ibid. xi. 776, 
Rot. Scot. ii. 437.) On Feb. 20, 1474-5, he was made a commissioner to settle 
the dispute about the fisheries in the Esk. (Rot. Scot. ii. 451.) On Aug. 20, 
1484, he was made a justice of peace and quorum for Ripon. (Beg. Bothernam, 
214 a.) And on Sept. 12, 1488, he was again appointed an ambassador to treat 
for peace with Scotland. (Bot. Scot ii. 487.) 

I find that Poteman was an executor of the wills of archbishop Neville and 
Ralph lord Greystock. He had a similar duty to do for Henry earl of North- 
umberland, who died in 1485, and who left to his " gossep, Mr. Wm. Poteman, a 
tonne of wine of Gascoigne yerelie duryng my lyve & his," and, after the earl's 
decease, " two tonnes." (Test Ebor. iii. 308.) He was also a benefactor to York 
minster. (Fabric Bolls, 217, 231.) 

* I can find no record of any monument to Poteman; and it is not known 
exactly where archbishop Neville was interred. 

f Among other gifts and privileges Richard III. "ordeigned 100 prests to be

priests were erected in 1484 (Fabric Rolls, 87), and a house or college for their 
reception seems to have been begun, if not completed. It was evidently pulled 
down and the materials sold on Richard's death.

* A son of John Vavasour, a younger son of the house of Haslewood, who

The testator was made a Justice of the C. P. in 1490, haying been previously 
Recorder of York. (Toss's Judges, v. 78-9.) The chauntry at Spaldington, about

The name of John Vavasour occurs frequently in the Law Reports of his 
time. His will is a characteristic one, and is confirmatory of the story that he 
was of a miserly disposition. He is mentioned frequently in the Plumpton Cor-

* The testator, whose connection with the family of Norton of Norton Conyers 
has not been traced, was the owner of the estate of Bilbrongh near York, to 
which Tillage and church he and his wife were great benefactors. He lies, as 
he desired, under an arch between the nave and a chantry chapel in Bilbrongh' 
church on the sooth side. His monument remains there. Between him and the 
wall is the black marble tomb of a much greater man, Thomas Lord Fairfax.

* The last of an old Holderness family, Martin of the Sea, or at Sea, is said to 
have been knighted by the Earl of Northumberland whilst serving in Scotland 
in 1482. (Poulson's Holderness, i. 196.) In 1471 he had taken an active part in 
opposing Edward IV. after he landed at Ravenspurn. (Restoration of King 
Edward IV., Camden Soc. 1838. p. 4.) 

In 1480, Martin de la Sea and Elizabeth Hawley were married. (Test Ebor. 
iii. 344.) This was perhaps a son of the testator who died young and childless. 
The estate of Barmston, which had come to the testator through his mother, 
passed away with his daughter to the Boyntons, who still possess it. I say 
nothing about the names of the testator's children or wife. The pedigree of the 
family in Poulson is wretched ; but it is perfection when we compare it wi^h 
that of the family of Boynton which immediately succeeds it. There is a line 
monument to the testator in Barmston church. 

When Sir Martin opposed Edward IV. he was greatly assisted by a priest of 
the name of John Westerdale. (Leland, Collect, ii. 503.) He was instituted 
vicar of Keyiogham in Holderness Oct. 3rd, 1467, and was so until 1479. 
(Reg. Geo. Neville, 96 a.) On June 15, 1454, John Westerdale of Beverley was 
ordained priest at York. (Reg. Wm. Booth.) He is probably the person who is 
mentioned in the will of Mr. William Westerdale, registrar of the court of York, 
in 1474. (Test Ebor. iii. 210.)

* To this little village the testator was a noble benefactor. In addition to 
many other kind offices he rebuilt the parish church. On Nov. 28, 1455, arch- 
bishop William Booth issued a commission to Mr. John Sendale, canon of York, 
Mr. William Langton, bacc. leg., Mr. Roger Burgh, bacc. deer., Mr. John 
•Worsley, in ntr. jur. bacc., and dan John Hovingham, vicar of Bilton, to inquire 
into the following case. Brian Roucliffe, patron of the living of Cowthorpe, has 
sent a petition to the archbishop " quia eccl. par. de Colthorp procul a villa de C. 
abolim erecta et ffidificata, ac via inter dictam eccl. et villam multum aquosa, 
lutosa et nociva, eundo et redeundo existit," that, therefore, he may be allowed to 
pull the old one down, add out of the old and new materials erect a new church 
m the village at his own cost. In the mean while he asks that the parishioners 
may hear service, and have the usual rites performed in a chapel within the 
manor house of the said Brian at Cowthorpe, until the new church is finished. The 
commissioners report favourably, and on Feb. 13, 1455-6, the archbishop sanctions 
the scheme, and grants an indulgence of 40 days to all those who assist the work. 
(Reg. Wm. Booth, 184-6.) On Aug. 17, 1458, the archbishop desired his suffragan, 
John bishop of Philippolis, to consecrate the new church, with a similar indul- 
gence. (Ibid. 368-9.)

With Brian, the father of George Bradford, the line of Bradford of Stanley,

John Bradford, the testator, was the u son John " mentioned in the will of 
William Bradford. A William Bradford was John's cousin and heir. I observe 
that in these wills " cousin and heir" generally means grandson; but it is 
capable, of course, of a far wider interpretation.

Henry Conyers is probably identical with Henry Conyers of Westlathes in 
Cleveland, esq. who made his will June 10, 1529, in which he desired to be

Jane, his sons Gawen and Thomas, and his daughter, the wife of Roger Pacoke.

Robert Conyers waB of Danby-upon-Yore, and married Anne daughter and 
heiress of Thomas Mountford of Hackforth, esq. William Conyers of Danby 
(mentioned in this will) was probably one of his sons. Simon, son and heir of 
Robert Conyers of Danby, married Elizabeth second daughter and co-heiress of 
Thomas Fulthorpe of Hipswell, and had by her an only child, Margaret, who 
became the wife of Henry Scrope, esq. of Spennithorne. (MSS. Taylor). 

Of Philip Conyers I know nothing. Margaret Ascough, the testator's sister, 
was probably the wife of one of the Ascoughs of Potgrange or Bedale. The 
marriage is new to that pedigree.

The testator does not appear in Mr. Hunter's list of the provosts of Rotherham 
college, nor is there any appointment of him as such in archbishop Rotherham 's 
Register. If, therefore, he is to be placed on the list, we muBt suppose that 
Greybern resigned and was re-appointed on Rawson's death. I give a more 
accurate list of the earlier provosts. They were obliged by statute to be Cam- 
bridge men. 

Mr. William Greybern, S. T. P. appointed the first provost in 1482-3, Edmund 
Carter and William Alynson being at the same time made the first Fellows. 
(Reg. Rotherham, 269.) In 1474 he was collated to the rectory of Sherington, 
Bucks. (Lipscombe's Bucks, iv. 336.) This he exchanged on Sept 20, 1486, 
with John Froctour for the rectory of Handsworth (Reg. Rotherham.) On March 
15, 1489-90, he was collated to a stall in St Sepulchre chapel, York. (Ibid. 103*.) 
This he resigned in 1501. (Reg. Savage, 21a.) 

His will is dated July 21, 1501. To be buried in Jesus* choir within Rother- 
ham church, if I die there. To the poor at my burial, 5L To each altar in the

Mr. Robert Cutler, S. T. B., collated March 4, 1508-9, on Hoton's retirement. 
(Reg. Bainbridge, 61 a.) On Oct. 24, 1497, letters dimissory were granted to

Mr. Robert Neville, S. T. B., collated Jan. 9, 1517-18, on the death of Cutler,

letters dimissory granted to him Dec. 9, 1505, being then A. B. (Reg. Savage, 
104 ft.) On Oct 2, 1506, Mr. Robert Neville was instituted to the rectory of 
Grove, Notts, on the presentation of Humphrey Hercy, esq. (Ibid. 82a.) He 
died in 1550, being at that time rector of Ordsall, vicar of Almondbury, pre- 
bendary of Bilton at York, to which he was collated Jan. 30, 1549-50 (Reg. 
Holgate, 32), and prebendary of Gaia Minor at Lichfield, to which he was 
Appointed in 1528. (Le Neve, i. 607.) He was possibly the person who was 
appointed to the living of Staunton, dioc. Salisbury, in 1530, (Phillipps' Wiltshire 
Incumbents, 201) and to the 12th stall at Canterbury in 1543 (Le Neve, i 61.) 

A very curious account of the destruction of Rotherham college is given in

* Precentor and canon residentiary of York. In 1456 I find a John Hert, a 
chantry-priest in the Minster, but whether he was the testator or not I am unable 
to say. On Not. 4, 1471, Hert, then chamberlain, was made sub-treasurer of the 
Minster (MS. Cotton, Vitellius, A ii. 149 J), an office which he gave up in 1488. 
On April 24, 1475, he was collated to a stall in St. Sepulchre's chapel (Res. 
Geo. Neville, ii. 14*); and, on Sept. 25, he was made sacrist of the same chapel, 
resigning his place in Nov. 1495. (Reg. Laur. Booth, 7 b.) On July 4, 1479, he 
was instituted to a prebend at Howden, which he held during his life. (Reg 
Laur. Booth, 52 b.) He had also the first stall at Hemingbrough, which he 
resigned in 1487. On Aug. 2, 1480, he was instituted to the rectory of Catwick 
(Reg. tede vac. 496 a), which he exchanged on Mav 23, 1482, for tie rectory of 
Everingham with Mr. Thomas Bentley. (Reg. Rotherham, 19 a.) On Dec. 10, 
1486, he was instituted to the rectory of Sutton upon Derwent. (Ibid. 146 a.) He 
was also vicar of St. Martin's, Coney-street, York, which he resigned in 1487. 

In York minster Hert held great preferment. On April 12, 1483, he was col- 
lated to the stall of Tockerington. (Reg. Rotherham, 96 b.) On Feb. 26, 1487-8, 
he was collated to that of Botevant. (Ibid. 103 a). On Dec. 13, 1490, he was collated 
to Fridaythorpe (Ibid. 104 a)*, and on June 23, 1494, to the precentorship. (Acta 
Capit.) He held this for a very short time. 

Hert's will is a curious one. He was buried in the nave of the Minster under a 
blue stone, four vards long, with a square brass plate and inscription. (Torre's 
York Minster, 161.)

LVUL THE WILL OF WILLIAM CAME OF NEWARK. 
[Reg. Test. y. 605 ft.] 

Aug. 4, 1496. William Came of Newarke. To be beried in 
the church of Blessid Mary Mawdlene in Newark. Toward the 
reparacion of the hy alter v li. To Margaret, the wyff of William 
Hill, a silver flate pece w* a knope of sylver ; a maser w* a playne 

• Thomas Barrow is a person who deserves something more than a passing 
record. 

He was one of the Yorkshire fellows of Eton in 1455 (Registrant Regale, viii.), 
after which he became fellow of King's-hall at Cambridge and doctor of laws 
there. (Fuller's Univ. Cant. 90.) In Sept. 1468 he was instituted to the vicarage 
of Chesterton, co. Cambridge, resigning it in 1472; and on Oct. 28, 1471, he was 
instituted to the living of CasUecamps. (MS. Baker, xxx. 42.) On Dec 29, 
1472, he was instituted to the rectory of Cottingham, co. York, on the king's pre- 
sentation. This he held till he died. (Reg. Geo. Neville, 152a.) On Jan. 13, 
1474-5, he was collated to the sacrist's prebend at Southwell, and a stall in St. 
Sepulchre chapel at York. (Ibid. ii. 3d.) He resigned both of these in March 
1474-5. On March 15, 1474, he was instituted to the rectory of Olney, Bucks, 
which he gave up in 1488. (Lipscombe's Bucks, iv. 306). On March 7, 1477-8, 
he was collated to the stall of Langtoft at York. (Reg. Laur. Booth, 5 b.) On 
Feb. 25, 1481-2, he was made examiner of witnesses in the court of York. (Reg* 
Rotherham, 206 J.) 

With Richard III. Barrow was a great favourite. He and Richard Barrow 
received from him an annuity of 70*. (MS. Harl. 433, 79 ft.) He was chancellor 
of the king's house (Fuller's Univ. Cant. 90); Master of the Rolls in 1483 (MS. 
Harl. 433 152), with a grant of two pipes of Gascoigne wine each year. (Fred, 
xii. 208.) On July 18, 1483, he was made archdeacon of Colchester, and acted 
as such till he died. (Newcourt, L 90/) On Sept. 20, 1484, he was made an 
ambassador to negotiate a peace with Scotland (Feed. xii. 235 ; Rot. Scotis, ii 
465.) On Aug. 1, 1486, he was appointed keeper of the privy seaL (Feed. xii. 
272; Dugd. Chron. 72.) There is a brief notice of him in Foss's Judges, ir. 
485-6, from which it appears that he was a prebendary of St. Stephen's, West- 
minster, a trier of petitions in parliament, and one of the masters in chancery. 

Barrow '8 will is at Doctors' Commons, but I have no notes from it. He died 
in 1501. He gave £240 toward the building of St. Mary's, Cambridge (Fuller's 
Univ. Cant. 90.) He left certain rents to the university for keeping his exequies 
(MS. Baker, at Cambridge, xxiv. 26).

* The dean was a younger son of Sir Robert Sheffield, a Lincolnshire knight, 
and the head of an ancient family. He first appears as beneficed in his native 
county. On Jan. 2, 1463, he was instituted to the rectory of Epworth. (MS. HarL 
6952, 88 J.) On April 28, 1477, he was allowed by papal dispensation to hold it 
with the rectory of Chesterford Magna in the diocese of London, which he held 
till his death, vacating at that time the rectory of Hogsthorpe, co. Lincoln. (Ibid. 
109 b ; Newcourt, ii. 133.) He was also connected with Lincoln cathedral, being 

?rebendary of Marston St. Lawrence from 1463 to 1477 ; and of Castor from 
477 until his appointment to the archdeaconry of Stow in Not. 1477. This he 
held till he died. (Le Neve, ii. 79, 127, 182.) 

At York Sheffield found a patron in archbishop Rotheram. On Feb. 16, 1483-4, 
being that prelate's chancellor, he was collated to the stall of Fridaythorpe (Beg. 
Botherham, 96 b\ which he gave up for the treasurership on July 13, 1485. 
(Ibid. 99a.) In May 1494 he was made dean (Ibid. 106-8) ; and he was allowed 
to hold in addition the stall of Tockerington, to which he was collated on June

* " Ricardus de York, merchaunt," was admitted to the freedom of the city of 
York, by purchase, in 1456. He was chamberlain in 1460, sheriff in 1465-6, lord 
mayor in 1469 and 1482, and was elected M.P. in 1473, 1482 (Dec. 13), 1483 
(Oct. 24), 1483-4 (Jan. 16), 1486, 1488 (Dec. 31), and 1490. 

In 1462, Richard York and his wife became members of the merchants' guild, 
and he was master of that guild, and of the company of merchants and mercers, 
in 1475. On January 15, 1466-7, being then mayor of the Staple of Calais, he 
was one of the guests at the great installation feast of archbishop Neville. 
When King Henry VII. visited York in July 1487, " in the Vigill of Saint Peter 
callid Advincle," he "dubbed my Lord Maier, called William Todde, and 
Richard York, alderman, knightes," they being the only citizens on whom he 
conferred that honour. — R. H. S. Sir Richard died in April 1498, and was 
buried in the church of St. John in Micklegate, where were many memorials of 
him and his family. Some of them still remain there. 

Sir Richard left a large family behind him. His first wife is said to hare been 
Joan Mauleverer, and she, no doubt, was the mother of his children. 

f This church has disappeared and the parish is annexed to that of St. Saviour.

LXXVII. THE WILL OP WILLIAM WORSLEY, DEAN OP ST. PAUL'S AND 
CANON OF YORK. 

[Reg. Test. Dec. et Cap. Ebor. iL, 22 b.] 

Feb, 12, 14th Henry VII. (1498-9). William Wonjey,* 
deane of the cathedrall chirch of Poules in London. My body 
to be buried in the cathedrall chirch of Poules, in the which syde 

• The testator was one of the Lancashire men who were brought into York- 
shire by the Booths. He was, it is believed, a son of Robert Worsley of Booth, 
in Eccles, by Margaret, daughter of Thomas Booth of Barton, a brother of the 
archbishops Booth. Robert and Seth Worsley were brothers of William. 
(Lane. MSS., voL xiii. F.R.R.) 

On March 30, 1453, he was collated to the stall of Norwell Overhall, at 
Southwell, which he held during his life. (Reg. Wm. Booth, 29*.) On July 23, 
1457, he was collated to the prebend of South Cave at York. (Ibid. 42). On 
Oct. 24, 1459, he had letters dimissory to receive the greater orders (Ibid. 207 b),

nave liverey of blake ; and also certeyn gownes of Make to be

and on Sept. 20, 1460, he was ordained priest. (Ibid.) He had already held the 
stall of Tachbrook at Lichfield, from 1449 to 1452. (Le Neve, i. 629.) 

On May 19, 1467, Worsley was instituted to the rectory of Eykering, Notts, 
(Reg. Geo. Neville, 91 b.) which he resigned in 1492-3. 

On Sept 28, 1476, he was admitted to the archdeaconry of Nottingham. (Reg. 
Dec. and Capit. Ebor.) This he held during his life. In Jan. 1478-9 he was 
made dean of St. Paul's, and he was also prebendary of Willesdon in the same 
church. (Le Neve, ii. 313, 451. Newcourt, i. 45.) From 1492-3 until 1496 he 
was archdeacon of Taunton. (Le Neve, i. 167.) 

Worsley was mixed up in the conspiracy of Perkin Warbeck, but after being 
examined his offence was overlooked. (Memorials of Henry VII. 69. Poly- 
dore Vergil, 592. Bacon's Henry VII. 75.) He died Aug. 14, 1499, and was 
buried in his cathedral church. (Dugdale's St. Paul's, n. e. 53. Gough's Sepul- 
chral Monuments, ii. 337. Weever, 368.) 

Several other members of the family of Worsley were connected with the county 
of York and its archbishops. 

On March 30, 1462, Benjamin Worsley, the archbishop's servant, was made 
keeper of the manor of Scrooby. (Reg. Wm. Booth, 1426.) After his death, his 
widow took the veil. (Test. Ebor. iii. 345.) 

On Dec. 9, 1458, John Worsley, commissary-general of the court of York, was 
collated to a stall in St. Sepulchre's chapel, York. (Reg. Wm. Booth, 45.) This 
he exchanged on Nov. 23, 1465, with William Betson for the prebend of 
" Kynwaston, alias Stonhall " in the royal chapel at Wolverhampton. (Reg. Geo. 
Neville, 3.) On March 9, 1460-1, he was instituted to the vicarage of Felkirk. 
(Reg. Wm. Booth, 407a.) 

On June 28, 1452, on the cession of William Worsley, Thomas Worsley was 
collated to the stall of Tachbrook at Lichfield, and he held it until 1501. (Le 
Neve, i. 629). On March 3, 1461-2, he was collated to the stall of Normanton 
at Southwell, in the person of Seth Worsley, esq., his proctor. (Reg. Wm. Booth, 
54.) He gave this up when, on the 13th of March, 1463-4, he was collated to 
the stall at the altar B.M.V. at Beverley. (Ibid. 58, 68 b.) On May 28, 1464, 
Thomas Worsley, canon of Beverley, was ordained deacon at York. (Ibid.) 
His will is as follows : — Jan. 11, 1500-1. Thomas Worsley, canon of St. John's 
church, Beverley. To be buried in the church of St. Andrew at Wimpole. To 
a priest, to celebrate a mass for me at Rome, 20*. To Charles Bothe, doctor, a 
nut. To the use of King's Hall, Cambridge, ij silver bowls. To Mr. Thos. 
Orston, my cousin, a Missal, a book called Matwnale Divinorum. To Robert 
Hamond, my Portifor after the Sarum use, a Manual, and Papilla Octdi. Cousin 
Alice Bell. [Pr. May 27, 1501.] (Reg. Moore, at Doctors' Commons.)

How are the persons mentioned in the following weird story related to the 
family at Haslewood ? 

On Sept. 16, 1488, archbishop Rotherham issues a commission to the rural 
dean of York, directing him to act in the following matter : William Vavasour 
of Pontefract, yeoman, otherwise called William Vavasour of Knottinglcy, gent., 
clerk, was charged before the king's justices in that -he on Friday before the 
feast of St. Thomas the Apostle, 18th Henry VII., at Haslewood, in a place 
called " Est Hesilwod park end," struck Richard Vavasour, his brother, " in 
posteriore parte dorsi sui usque ad cor suum cum j gestro vocato a hyngard," of 
which blow he instantly died. He was found guilty, and, being a clerk, was handed 
over to us. He now denies his guilt. The rural' dean reports that he has suffi- 
ciently purged himself. (Reg. Rotherham, 313a.) 

On Sept. 5, 1481, archbishop Rotherham granted letters dimissory to Mr. 
William Vavasour, bachelor or arts, that he might proceed to minor orders. 
(Reg. Rotherham, 203a.) 

On Aug. 14, 1481, Henry Vavasour, clerk, was instituted to the rectory of 
Terrington on the presentation of Sir Thomas Metham. (Reg. Rotherham, 168/z). 

On Oct. 5, 1484, he was instituted to the chantry of St. Nicholas at Haslewood, 
on the presentation of Sir Henry Vavasour. (Ibid. 117 a).

* This ancient family, of which next to nothing is known, had its residence 
at Sothill Hail in the parish of Dewsbury. There are now no traces of the 
Sothills there save the name of the place and a fragment of a grave-stone in the 
garden of the vicarage-house. The present will adds largely to the stock of 
information that we possess respecting the Sothills, and it is of great value as a 
specimen of the dialect of the country. It is copied with the most minute 
accuracy. 

On June 16, 1486, administration of John Sothill, sen., of Sothill, par. Dews- 
bury, esq., was granted, to John Sothill of Mirfield, esq. (Reg. Test. v. 256a.) 
This, I presume, is the testator's father. 

A branch of this family settled subsequently at North Deighton, coming 
thither out of Leicestershire. I have some original evidence about the Leicester- 
shire family which always kept up its connection with the West Riding. In the

"Henry Sothill of Stokeston, a second brother, and of the house of Sothill 
Hall." This is not correct. The pedigree should stand as follows: — 

Henry Sothill, a lawyer, a younger son of Gerard Sothill of Redburne, co. 
Lincoln, married Anne, only daughter of John Boyville of Stockfaston, co. 
Leicester, and eventually the heiress of that place. His eldest son, John Sothill, 
was contracted in marriage in 1463-4, to Elizabeth, one of the two co-heirs of 
William Plumpton of Plumpton, esq., her sister marrying Sir John Roucliffe of 
Cowthorpe, knt. (Plumpton Con*, var. loe.) 

John Sothill, esq., the husband of Elizabeth Plumpton, made his will by word 
of mouth June 2nd, 1493, being then of Stockfaston. He desires to be buried 
in the chapel of St. Botulph at Stockfaston, near the grave of his father. 
The residue is left to Elizabeth his wife, dame Anne his mother, ' Robert, 
Henrv, Gerard, and Henry Sothill his brothers. John Harrington and William 
Babthorpe esqrs., his executors. [Pr. Oct. 7, 1494.] (Reg. Vox at Doctors' 
Commons.) 

The will of the widow of John Sothill, Elizabeth Plumpton, runs as fol- 
lows : " Dame Elisabeth Sothill. To be buried at the Gray Freres at London 
in the same place that my sone Henry Sotehill is buryed ; and my hert to be 
take out of my body, and buryed at Stockfaston by my housbande. My bro r 
in lawe, Robert Sothill, to pay to the inariage of my doughter Elizabeth, as he 
hath promysed by hys f eith and truthe of the dett that he owith me a c li.

The testatrix died Sept. 21, 1506, leaving as her heirs the twin infant- 
daughters of her deceased son Henry, who were only a year old on May 21, 1506. 
(Plumpton Corr.) Henry Sothill of Stockfaston, esq., made his will Feb. 16, 
1505-6, desiring to be buried in the church of the Gray Friars, London, if he 
dies there. To Joan, his wife, he leaves his lands at " Ardyslowe," co. York, 
for life. His wife, Sir Richard Empson, knt., and John Harrington, esq., are 
his executors. " I owe Thomas Sothill for the bevng of a chief rent in Ardys- 
ley, 10/." I owe my uncle Henry Sothill, 50/. ior performing my grandames' 
will. [Pr. 16th May, 1506.] (Reg. Holgrave at Doctors' Commons.) 

Gerard Sothill died Dec 25, 1528, and was buried atEuston,co. Suffolk. (The 
Topogr. et Gen. i. 284.) 

Joan, wife of Henry Sothill, was a daughter of the notorious Sir Richard 
Empson. After her husband's death, she re-married Sir William Pierrepoint of 
Holme, co. Notts, knt. Joan Sothill, her eldest daughter, married John, a younger 
son of Sir Marmaduke Constable of Flamborough, afterwards Sir John Con- 
stable of Kinalton, co. Notts. Elizabeth Sothill, the younger sister, married Sir 
William Drury of Hawstead, co. Suffolk. (Plumpton Corr. 208.) From Robert 
Sothill, a younger brother of Henry, the Sothills of North Deign ton descend.

v. 316 ft.) 

From this marriage there were four children. 1. Sir John Darell of Sessay,

2. Thomas Darell, brother and heir of Sir .John, who died s.p. 17th Henry VII. His 
wife's name was Margery, and she seems to be a Strangways of East Harlsey. 

3. Marmaduke Darell, who also died s. p. They had an only sister, Joan, who 
carried the estates and the representation of her ancient house to the family 
of Dawney.

XCVn. THE WILL OF DAME JANE STRANGWAYS. 
[Reg. Test. vi. 16 &.] 

Oct 28, 1500. In the name of the Almyghty God, the 
blessyd Trinite, the blessyd Lady and Virgyn Synt Mary, Amen. 
I dame Jayne Strangwais,* wydowe. Ifit forten me to decesse 

said to have married Agnes, daughter of Sir William Ingleby of Ripley. This 
is his will: — 

Everingham, May 10, 1490. John Sothill of Eyeringham, esq. To be buried 
in the choir of the church of Everingham. Alice his wife, Sir Marmaduke 
Constable, knt., and John Hert, canon residentiary- of York, are his executors. 
Witness, Henry Sothill, &c. [Pr. Nov. 28, 1494.) (Reg. Test. v. 452*.) The 
Inquisition on nis death shews that George Sothill was his son and heir, being 
thirty years old* on his father's death. (The 6am e George was cousin and heir 
of Henry Sothill of Eyeringham, who died 16th Noy. 16 Hen. VII.) (Orig.) 

This George Sothill was an imbecile (fatuus) and his estates were for some 
time in the hands of the Crown. He died in 1502, and it was found that he 
left two sisters and co-heiresses, Mary wife of Sir John Normanville, knt., 
then aged 34, and Barbara wife of Sir Marmaduke Constable, aged 28. (Orig.) 
Marmaduke Constable was the second son of Sir Marmaduke Constable of 
Flamborough. His brother, Sir John Constable, married another heiress of 
Sothill, a daughter of Henry Sothill of Stockfaston, esq. The Constables 
became the owners of Eyeringham, and through them the present Lord Henries 
is its possessor. 

* A Cheshire lady and a Yorkshire woman only by marriage. She was a 
daughter of Sir Richard Aston of Aston, and widow of Roger Dutton, esq.

She became the second wife of Sir Richard Strangways, knt. who died in 1488, 
and, bearing his name, she died. Her will was made in the house of the Friars 
Preachers at York, wherein she was a sojourner. It is chiefly filled with religious 
bequests, and the testatrix mentions very few of her kith and kin. I shall have 
to speak elsewhere of the noble house of Strangways. 

Sir Richard Strangways died April 13th, 3rd Henry VII. leaving Sir James 
Strangways, knt. his son and heir, who was then 28.

* The father of archbishop Crannier. The family of Cranmer, which is a 
very ancient one, came into the possession of Aslacton in the parish of Whatton 
by a marriage with the heiress of the Aslactons. The Cranmers, with all their 
ancient blood, were never wealthy. It will be observed that the patrimony of 
the future archbishop was only twenty shillings a-year, with the possibility of 
its being doubled, which never came to pass. 

From a letter in an old volume of the Gentleman's Magazine I take the follow- 
ing description of the testator's monument in Whatton church. " Against the 
north-east pillar (of the nave) is fixed up a white slab with the figure of a man 
in flowing hair and gown, and a purse at his right side, his head on a cushion, 
and round him on a ledge, Hie jacet Thomas Cranmer armiger, qui obiit 
vicesimo septimo die memis Maii, anno Domini m or cente*imo primo, cvjus 
aninup propicietur Dem. Amen. On the right side of his head, five fusils in 
fess, which in Thoroton's time were charged with as many escallops, being the 
arms of Aslacton: on the left, a chevron between three cranes." 

I shall have something to say elsewhere about archbishop Cranmer's unworthy 
son.

the person who was collated to the rectory of Foston on Feb. 18, 1493-4. (Reg. 
Rotherham, 78*.) 

There were one or two noted families of the name in Westmorland. The fol- 
lowing notices relate to one that was settled in York. 

In 1445, Mr. John Lancastre clerk, son of John Lancastre, tailor, York, was 
admitted to his freedom. Robert Lancastre, clerk, son of John Lancastre, tailor, 
was living in 1447. In 1457, John Lancastre merchant, son of William Lancastre 
clerk, was made free. In 1472, Mr. Nicholas Lancastre, clerk and merchant, and, 
in 1478, Richard Lancastre clerk, sons o( John Lancastre merchant, became 
freemen by patrimony. The above Nicholas was admitted into the Merchants' 
Guild in 1472, and was constable of the Merchants' Company 1474. As " Nicholas 
Lancastere, in ntroqne jure baccalaureus," he was elected common clerk of the 
city of York on Feb. 3rd, 1476-7, vice Richard Derwentwater, and he resigned 
that office in 1480. In 1483, he occurs as one of the king's council (Extracts 
from York Records, 207). Nicholas Lancastre, LL.D. was elected an alderman 
April 10th, 1484, filled the office of Lord Mavor in 1485 and 1493, was returned 
M.P. for the city of York October 16th, 1487, and died in 1501. In his will, 
dated January 10th, 1500-1 [Pro. Sept. 1, 1501], he desires to be buried in the 
church of St. Michael-le-Belfrey. — R. H. S.

From the Laton chartulary I derive the following notes. The eldest son of 
the testatrix was Thomas Laton, whose marriage contract with Margaret, 
daughter of Richard Clervaux, esq. of Croft, was dated Jan. 12, 1458. The issue 
of this alliance was an only daughter Anne, who was contracted on Jan. 18, 5th 
Hen. VIL, to Edward, son and heir of Reginald Warcop, esq., and a settlement 
of the estates of the young lady's father was made, the dower of Eleanor, his 
mother, being untouched. Thomas Laton is said to have married, secondly, Anne, 
daughter of Robert Mauleverer, but this statement requires farther proof.

CXV. THE WILL OF SIR RANtJLPH PIGOT OF CLOTHERHAM, KNT. 
[Reg. Teat. vi. 74 &.] 

May 26, 1503. Ranulphus Pigott,* miles. Sep. in eccl. coll. 
B. Petri Ripon. Ministris chori, cuilibet calayber ameysse, 
viij d. Cuilibet saule-prest iiij d. Fabricae eccl. de Ripon x boves

certeine that I never knew hym for none, nor never understude hyme as oone ;'

Baide aggrement and concord e." 

On January 31st, 1486-7, William Todd was re-elected alderman, and a few 
days afterwards was chosen lord mayor. During his year of office he repaired, 
at his own cost, a considerable portion of the city walls adjoining Fishergate 
Bar, and, on July 31st, received the honour of knighthood from King Henry the 
Seventh. On December 31st, 1488, he was elected M.P., and he was again 
returned in 1490. 

In 1465 William Todd and his wife were admitted into the Merchants' Guild, 
and he was constable of the Merchants' Company in 1471, 1472 and 1475, and 
master in 1477 and 1478. 

Sir William Todd was thrice married. The name of his first wife, who was 
living in 1465, is not known. His second wife was Margaret, widow of Thomas 
EckiTsell of Scarborough. In her will, dated 30th July, 1483 (Pro. 23 Sep. 1483), 
she desires to be buried in the monastery at Whitby. (Reg. Test. v. 199.) The 
third wife of Sir William Todd was Elizabeth Eland, of Hull. Licence to 
marry them was granted to the curate of the chapel of the Holy Trinity, Hull, 
January 24th, 1484-5. (Test. Ebor. iii. 349.) R. H. S.

This note bears the initials of my lamented friend, Mr. J. R. Walbran, of 
Ripon, who died very recently. His death is the greatest loss which English 
archaeology has sustained since that of Mr. Hunter. I shall speak elsewhere of 
his merits and his works.

f The testator was one of those ecclesiastics who were high in the favour of

required to preach in York minster in the fifth year of his regency. He was 
also surveyor of the works at Great St. Mary's in 1487. (Ath. Cant. i. 7.) 

In the diocese of York Trotter held several high offices. On April 29, 1489,

Dunnington at York. (Ibid. 104 a.) In 1491 he was collated to the prebend of

preserved in their allotted places.

The testator, Edward Cresacre, mentions several of his neighbours at Arksey. 
His godson, Edward Cresacre, was the last of his name. He left an only 
daughter who became the wife of the only son of the famous Sir Thomas More. 
The name of Cresacre More preserved the memory of the ancient owners of 
Barnborough. 

Upon one chapter in the history of his family the subdean of York conld not

* There is some difficulty in finding out who this gentleman was. In the 
account of the descent of the manor of Badsworth in Mr. Hunter's South York- 
shire he is said to be of Spaldington, the father of Sir Peter, and the grand- 
father of John Vavasour, esq. This, however, is quite wrong, as in the obituary 
of the Vavasours of Spaldington, printed in this volume (p. 91), William Vava- 
sour, the grandfather of John, is said, on irrefragable authority, to have died in 
1495. On the same page there is an extract from his will dated in that year. 
Mr. Hunter has been misled by the statement of Beckwith, making William 
Vavasour, who died in 1495, the husband of the heiress of Badsworth, whereas 
the owner of Badsworth was the present testator. This marriage is mentioned 
in a note of mine at p. 91, which must be regarded as a statement of the opinion 
of Beckwith and Hunter, and not as a matter of fact. The alliance with 
Mallory is probably correct. 

Who then was the testator ? He was evidently a member of the house of 
Haslcwood. In his will he mentions his parents Henry and Joan. Now these 
are the Christian names of Sir Henry Vavasour (and his wife), who died in 1500. 
(See his will pp. 166-7.) In the will of Sir Henry, William his son and heir is 
mentioned who is not otherwise accounted for, and in a window in Badsworth 
church there were the figures of a Vavasour and his lady, the lady bearing on 
her robe the arms of Gascoigne. The wife of the Sir Henry Vavasour just 
alluded to was a Gascoigne of Gawthorpe. 

Now the father of the testator was " squier," not knight, whilst in this will 
there is no mention whatever of the Haslcwood or his brothers. These objec-

But he may have been his brother, the son of Henry Vavasour, esq., who died

may assume therefore that the window at Badsworth which has been alluded to 
was given by Sir Henry in consideration of his brother. 

The testator married Isabel, dau. and heiress of Robert Urswick, esq., through 
whom he became the owner of Badsworth. According to Dodsworth, (MS. 
Oxon. iii. 301,) when she married him, she was the widow of — Presteman. 
They seem to have had no issue. In what manner the estate of Badsworth 
passed to the Vavasours of Spaldington, I do not know. It is evident from 
the conclusion of his will, that the testator was on bad terms with at least one 
of his nephews of the house of Haslewood. They had nothing to do with Bads- 
worth, which was probably sold and bought by the Vavasours of Spaldington 
with the money of their rich uncle, the justice. 

* Several of these trustees were distinguished men. With Christopher Urswick

James Harrington was the son of Robert Harrington and Isabel Balderston. 
(Hunter's South Yorkshire ii. 402. Whitaker's Richmondshire, ii. 251.) In his 
early life he was in some political trouble, for he dared to be a Yorkist when the 
Lancastrian interest was too paramount. On May 27, 1496, he was instituted to. 
the rectory of Badsworth on the presentation of Thomas earl of Derby, con- 
stable of England, and Joan, widow of Sir John Pilkington, knt. (Reg. Rother- 
ham, 134 J.) This he held for his life. On July 21st, 1497, the archbishop 
granted him letters dimissory. (Ibid. 262 b.) On Oct. 29, 1501, he was instituted 
to the rectory of Tankersley, which he also held during his life. (Reg. Savage, 
10&.). On Aug. 20, 1506, he was collated to a stall in St. Sepulchre chapel at 
York (Ibid. 29k), which he gave up in 1511. On Jan. 27, 1506-7, he was 
collated to the stall of Husthwaite at York. (Ibid. 30 a.) On July 13th, gcg., 
he was made subdean (Ibid. 31 aJ); and on Jan. 29th in the following year, by a 
rapid and most unprecedented step, he was advanced to the deanery. (Acta 
Capit. Ebor.) On March 30th, 1509, he was made prebendary of Bugthorpe. 
(Reg. Bainbridge, 31 b.) 

Dean Harrington did not hold his high office for a long time, and he suffered 
from ill-health before he died. On Dec. 2nd, 1510, he is excused by the 
chapter from coming to the Minster during his greater residence, as he is so ill 
that he cannot go up to or leave his stall. (Acta Capit. Ebor.) He was buried 
in his cathedral on the festival of the Innocents, 1512, and on April 26, 1513, 
Mr. Thomas Wolsey, his successor, administered to his effects. (Ibid.) Among 
the fabric accounts for 1515-16, is an item which shews that the chapter paid 
46*. 8d. for a through stone of marble, and an inscribed plate of brass to lay 
over dean Harrington. (Fabric Rolls, 97.)

I find Rowkshaw corresponding with Sir Robert Plumpton in 1489 (Plumpton 
Corr., 82-3), and a trustee for the family of Clifton, 22nd Edward IV. (Thoroton's 
Notts, 55.) But it was with the noble house of Percy that he was especially 
connected. He was indebted to it for much of his preferment, and it is probable 
that he was a retainer in the earl's household. Henry Earl of Northumberland 
was killed in a popular outbreak in April, 1489, and this outrage produced a well- 
known elegy from the laureate, Skelton. The poet endorses nis dirge with the 
following lines, which are written in his easily-flowing Latinity. 

Tetrastichon Skelton Laureati ad magistrum Rukshaw, Sacra Theologias 
egregium Professorem. 

Accipe nunc demum, doctor celeberrime Rukshaw, 

Carmina, de calamo quae ceciderc meo ; 
Et quamqnam placid is non sunt modulata camaenis, 
Sunt tamen ex nostro pectore prompta pio. 

Vale feliciter viroium laudatissime 1

Erobably the blue lion of their arms that decked the bed-covering which he 
equeathed to Lowthorpe church. He had letters of fraternity from the order 
of Sempringham, and desires that the customary messenger be sent round to the 
various monasteries of that limitation to obtain* the promised prayers.

* Sir Robert Brackenbury was the well-known lieutenant of the Tower in the 
reign of Richard III. He was a member of an old Durham family, and was one 
of those trusty North-countrymen who clung to Richard in all his troubles and 
died with him at Bosworth. The testatrix found shelter under the wing of the 
Howards. 

Sir Robert left two daughters and co-heirs— Joan, the eldest, married John 
Penne, esq. The name of the other and her history have been unknown till this 
will was discovered. 

I add some notices of two other members of the same family : 

John Brackenburgh became vicar of Heston diocese of London, in 1480, and

at Lincoln, which he resigned in 1485. (Ibid. ii. 206.) These appointments seem

CXL. THE WILL OP GEORGE FITZHUGH, DEAN OF LINCOLN. 

[Reg. Test. Dec. et Cap. ii. 55 a.'] 

Georgius Fizthugh,* decanus eccl. cath. B. M. Lincoln, fidelis 
in Domino Jhesu Christo. In primis, juxta sanctam fidem 
catholicam, lego animam meam, et spiritum meum commendo in 
misericordiam et manus Dei Omnipotentis, Sanctissimae Trinita- 
tis, Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti, in fide firma et spe sancta 
redemptionis aaternae per eandem Dei misericordiam, et suavissi- 
mum meritum passionis gloriosae Domini nostri Jhesu Christi ; 
ex Cujus sacrosanctis vulneribus per pretiosi sanguinis eftusi- 
onem copiosam, et intercessionem Suae genetricis B.V.M., et 
Omnium Sanctorum, spero firmiter lavacrum et remissionem 

* A younger son of the lordly house of Fitzhugh. His father was Henry 
Fitzhugh, his mother Alice, daughter of Richard Neville earl of Salisbury. He 
was pushed forward in life with that scandalous haste which marked the rise of 
so many members of noble families. On the 21st of May, 1475, he was collated 
by his kinsman, archbishop Neville, to the stall of Weighton at York. (Reg. 
Neville, ii. 17 a.) He was at this time only thirteen years of age ! On April 

27, 1476, Sixtus IV. gave him leave to hold a benefice, when he was sixteen, he 
being of noble birth, and the cousin of Edward IV. (Reg. Geo. Neville.) Fitz- 
hugh, however, it will be seen, had already taken time by the forelock. In 1477, 
when he was fifteen, he had a presentation to the rich rectory of fiedale, but it 
was a faulty one and nothing came of it. (Reg. arch id. Richmond.) In 1478 
he was admitted B.A. at Cambridge, with liberty to go out M.A. when he would, 
and to be regent or not as he thought fit. In 1483 he was D.D. (Ath. Cant. i. 10 ; 
Hawes' and Loder's Framlingham, 220; Lei. Coll. v. 388). In 1480 he was 
elected master of Pembroke coll. which he held during his life, and in 1496 and 
1501 he was made chancellor of the University. (Le Neve iii. 601.) 

On March 15, 1478-9, he was instituted to the living of Wintringham on his 
mother's presentation (MS. Harl. 6952, 103 a), and, on April 18, 1482, he was 
instituted to the rectory of Bingham, Notts. (Reg. Rotherham, 167 ft). On Sept. 

28, 1485, he was collated to the prebend at St. Catharine's altar at Beverley 
(Ibid. 100 ft) which he resigned in 1488. 

His chief preferments were at Lincoln. From 1474-5 to 1477 he was pre- 
bendary of Fmpingham (Le Neve, ii. 147). In 1486 he became prebendary of 
Croperdy there. (Ibid. ii. 140.) In Oct. 1483, he reached his highest honour, 
the deanery of Lincoln, which he held until his death on November 20th, 1505. 
(Ibid. ii. 33.) He kept a large household (Ath. Cant. i. 522), and along with 
his mother was a contributor to the stock of vestments which belonged to the 
cathedral. (Dugd. Mon. vi. 1279, 1283-5.) 

There are some notices of George . Fitzhugh in Ath. Cant. i. 10, 522 ; 
Churton's Lives of the Founders of Brasenose College, 121 ; Lei. Coll. v. 388 ; 
Dugdale's Baronage, i. 405 ; Hist. Univ. Cant. i. 58.

daughter of William Bosvile. He left an only daughter, Margaret, but the great 
part of his estate went to his nephew, Richard Tempest, who married an 
heiress of Boiling. This will is full of new and curious information.

* The younger of die two illegitimate sons of Sir William Plumpton. He

In Dei nomine, Amen. xvij mo die mensis Julii, anno 
Domini millesimo quingentesimo septimo, Ego, Rogerus La- 
burue,* Divina permissione Karliolensis episcopus, compos 
mentis, et sanae memorise, condo testamentum meum in hunc 
modum. Inprimis lego animam meam Deo Omnipotenti, Beate 
Marias Virgini, et Omnibus Sanctis, corpusque meum sepelien- 
dum in ecclesia parochiali Sancti Jacobi Apostoli juxta Charing 
Crosse, cum mortuariis meis debitis et de jure consuetis. Item 
volo quod Fratres monasteriorum, Praedieatorum, videlicet, et 
Minor um, vocentur ut intersint exequiis meis die sepulturae meae ; 

* The testator was probably one of the Leybournes of Cunswick in Westmer- 
land, but on this point there is no direct evidence. (Nicolson and Burn, i. 144.) 
Fellow of Pembroke, Cambridge, and proctor for the University in 1488: D.D. 
(Lei. Coll. v. 389 ; Hawes and Loder's Framlingham, 220 ; Ath. Cant.) His 
great patron seems to have been Richard Fox, bishop of Durham, in whose 
diocese he held the following preferments. The rectory of Sedgfield in 1491 
(Surtees, iii. 32); the rectory of Wolsingham, 1497-9 (Hutchinson's Durham, iii. 
299), and that of Longnewton (Surtees, iii. 217) ; the temporal chancellorship 
of the diocese 1499-1501 (MSS. Surtees); the arch-deaconry of Durham 1499- 
1504 (Le Neve, iii. 304) ; and the mastership of Kepier hospital, 1501. (Sur- 
tees, iv. part ii.) 

Ley bourne was also prebendary of Orindall at York from 1501 to 1503 (Le 
Neve, iii. 191), and master of Pembroke at Cambridge 1505-7 (Ibid. iii. 673). 
From 1504 to 1607 he was bishop of Carlisle (Ibid. iii. 240), but died soon, 
" before he c d express his good intentions to his colledge or cathedrall." (Fuller's 
Worthies, i. 236.) His will is registered at Doctors' Commons, but without the 
codicil. He seems to have died overwhelmed with debt. 

On Sept. 21, 1507, the chapter of York empower Mr. Walter Redman S. T. P., 
provost of Grey stock, Cuthbert Conyers, bachelor of decrees and rector of 
llutton Forrest, William Husband, rector of Longnewton, William Holgill, 
vicar of Bromticld, dioc. Carlisle, and Alexander Dawson of Grcystock, notary, 
to collect the Bishop's goods, &c.

CLVII. THE WILL OF ROBERT LASCELLBS OF BRAKENBUBGH, ESQ. 
[Reg. Test. vii. 32 a, etc.] 

Feb. 20, 1507-8. Egbert Lassals* of Brakenbarghe. To be

* The testator was the son of Robert Lascelles of Sowerby, near Thirsk. (See 
Test. Ebor. iii. 197-8.) He was twice married. His first wife was Eleanor,

seems to have been Margaret, daughter of James Danby esq., a younger son, I

the North Riding antiquary. 

The eldest son of the testator was Sir Roger Lascelles, who made his will in 
1551. His grandson, Sir Thomas Lascelles, was a spendthrift, and ran through 
his property. The house and estate of Brakenburgh then came into the 
market. The following extract from a letter from Ambrose Appleby, an agent 
of Lord Cavendish, to his master in 1618, will give some idea of the extent of a 
house of which not a trace remains.

courte, wherein is a f ayre well, which serveth y* house with verie clere and good

CLXHI. THE WILL OF MB. MAKTIN COLLINS, TREASURER OF YORK. 

[Reg. Bainbridge, 135-6.] 

August 18, 1508. Martinus Colyns,* thesaurarius eccl. 
cath. Ebor., canonicusque residentiarius in eadem. In casu quo 
me in partibus borealibus mori contigerit, corpus meum human- 



great 
Henr 



* The testator was high in the favour of archbishop Rotherham, and held 
reat preferment in the cathedral and diocese of York. He, with Hugh Trotter, 
lenry Carnebull, and one or two others constituted the group of ecclesiastics 
who did most of the work and occupied the chief positions in the diocese of 
York at this time. 

On Jan. 25, 1493-4, Collins was instituted to the rectory of Wilford, Notts. 
(Reg. Rotherham, 181*.) Between 1490 and 1497 he was rector of Thingden, 
Northants. (Bridges' Northants, ii. 260.) On March 11, 1495 6, he was insti- 
tuted to the rectorv of Barton in Fabip, Notts. (Reg. Rotherham, 90*) which he 
held during his life. On July 9, 1499, was collated to the prebend at the altar 
of St. Stephen at Beverley. (Ibid. 110*.) On Sept. 29, in the same year, he 
was instituted to the vicarage of Leeds. (Ibid. 139 a. ; Vicaria Leodiensis, 25-6 ; 
Loidis and Elmete, 20-1.) This he resigned, and on June 27, 1500, an annual 
pension of 20/. was assigned to him from it. (Reg. tede vac. 500 *.) On Oct. 
2, 1500, he was admitted to the mastership of the hospital in Bootham, York. 
(Ibid. 501 *.) On Jan. 20, 1502 3, he was instituted to the living of Kirkby in 
Cleveland (Reg. Savage, 19a.), and on Dec. 5, 1505, he was collated to the stall 
of Palishall at Southwell. (Ibid. 29a.) On April 12, 1501, and Dec. 3, 1608, 
he was made official of the court of York. (Regg. Savage, 1 b. ; and Bain- 
bridge, la.) 

In the cathedral of York Collins held the following offices : On Nov. 7, 1494, 
he was admitted to the stall of Bugthorpe (Acta Capit. Ebor.), and on Nov. 30 
$eq. f he was collated to that of Apesthorpe. (Reg. Rotherham, 106 a.) On Nov. 
18, 1496, Collins was advanced to the dignity of precentor (Ibid. 108 a), the 
prebend of Driffield going with it ; whilst, on Sept. 12, 1503, he was collated to 
the treasurership, in which office he died. (Reg. Savage, 24 a.) 

It will be seen from the present will that Collins was a munificent friend to 
the minster, to which he was bound by so many ties. See Fabric liolls, pp. 
216, 309. 

Collins was buried in York minster, in the position that he had selected for 
himself, under "a blue marble stone, about four yards long, with the four 
Evangelists in as many cinque -foils at corners ; towards the foot two escocheons 
of this charge, viz., three martlets on a bend ; and at the head a brass plate " 
bearing an inscription showing that Collins died on Feb. 4, 1508-9. (MS. 
Torre, 162 ; Drake's Eburacum, 501.) 

The brother of the testator, John Collins, alias Twyford, was instituted at 
his brother's presentation to the vicarage of St. Mary Bishophill Junior, in 
York, on Oct. 28, 1504. (Acta Capit. Ebor.) This he resigned, on account of old 
age, in 1522, receiving from it an annual pension of 4/. 6*. Sd. It is more than 
probable that the two brothers were natives of Twyford, near Melton Mowbray t 
in Leicestershire.

* These papers are strictly connected with the executorship of Martin Collins, 
and are rolled up in the large paper inventory of the effects of that ecclesiastic. 
Collins and Thomas Dalby seem to have been the Archbishop's executors, who 
died on the 3rd of September 1507, but these papers extend over several years 
beyond that date. The grand inventory of the goods of the Archbishop does 
not exist in York. I shall allude to these documents elsewhere in my life of the 
Archbishop. My object in printing them here is to place them permanently on 
record.

Archbishop Savage have not been recovered. The inventory would have exhi-

the King paid himself by taking a large portion of his effects.

DISPENSATIONS FOR MARRIAGE, MARRIAGE 
LICENCES, ETC. 

In the third volume of the Testamenta, pp. 311-375, there is 
a list of all these documents that are to be found in the Northern 
Registers between 1374 and 1531. I now complete the list by 
adding thoso which occur in the earlier registers, together with 
a few that were accidentally omitted in their proper places. 

1308, Nov. 29. Licence from the archbishop of York, citing 
letters from Cardinal Berengarius, the papal penancer, for Roger 
de Mannesherth and Petronilla do Kingthorp "quod possint 
simul stare in matrimonio contracto." — Beg. archiep. Greenfield, 
i. 906. 

1311-12, Feb. 16. Licence from Robert Pickering, canon of 
York and vicar-general, for John bishop of Lincoln to receive 
the vow of chastity of Alice widow of Sir Richard de Bingham 
knt — Ibid. ii. 146 a. 

1312-13, March 2. Commission from William archbishop 
of York to Richard bishop of Durham to receive the vow of 
chastity of dame Amabilla widow of Sir Robert de Cleseby, knt. 
Ibid. ii. 176 b; and Beg. Kellawe, 75 a. 

1316, Dec. 5. Commission to David " Recreensis episcopus " 
to receive the vow of chastity from Margaret widow of John 
Chaumon of Colton. — Beg. sede vac. 86 b. 

1318-19, Feb. 16. Dispensation sanctioning a marriage that 

has taken place between William son of Nicholas of Melton and 

Christiana his wife, they being cousins. On inquiry the relation- 

•ship is thus shown. Anketinus, called the deacon, has a son 

Thomas and a daughter Agnes. Thomas is the father of Ralph, 

VOL. iv. z 



338 TESTAMEKTA 

called the clerk ; Ralph is the father of another Ralph who is 
the sire of Matilda the mother of William. On the other side 
Agnes is the mother of Alexander Paslew who is the father of 
Geoffrey the father of Christiana. A dispensation from John 
XXII. is cited, dated at Avignon, Jan. 13, 1317-18.-22^. 
archiep. Melton, 275 a. 

1324, Nov. 23. Absolution of Robert de Ripon, chaplain, 
from a sentence of suspension for three years for celebrating a 
clandestine marriage between Nicholas, the carpenter of Ripon, 
and Isold de Skelton.— Ibid. 82 b. 

1325, Dec. 23. Absolution of Robert de Darleton, chaplain, 
for celebrating a clandestine marriage between Thomas Mor- 
tayn and Margaret Haunsard. — Ibid. 5666. 

1327-8, Jan. 27. Dispensation sanctioning the marriage which 
has taken place between Geoffrey le Clerk of Sibthorp and Alma 
daughter of Roger de Bottlesfora. Related in the fourth degree. 
Issued at Avignon, July 14, tenth John XXII. — Ibid. 3606. 

1328-9, Feb. 2. Archbishop Melton, at Cawood, receives the 
vow of chastity from Margery widow of Sir Adam de Swilling- 
ton, knt.— Ibid. 17 5 b. 

1329, April 17. Absolution of Thomas de Lelle, rector of 
Goxhill, from suspension for three years for marrying clan- 
destinely Robert de Lelle of Goxhill and Alice dicta Spmay.— 
Ibid. 311a. 

1334-5, Jan. 18. Dispensation sanctioning a marriage which 
has taken place between Sir Geoffrey Lutterell, knt, and Agnes 
daughter of Sir Robert de Sutton, knt 3rd and 4th degrees. 
Issued at Avignon by John XXII. Oct 19, anno pont 16. — 
Ibid. 382 a. 

1338-9, Jan. 23. Commission to the abbat of Thornton to 
receive the vow of chastity of Alice Attesee, widow of John 
Attesee of Ravenser. — Ibid. 5496. 

1339-40, March 24. Commission to John de Levyngton, 
S.P.P., an Augustinian Friar, to receive the vow of chastity 
of Christiana widow of John de Threlkeld. — Reg. John Kirkby 
episc. Carlisle j 208 a.
